title.rendered: Pan-Mass Challenge makes record-breaking $78 million gift to drive Dana-Farber’s progress against cancer

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Michael Quinn
Photography by Pan-Mass Challenge

The Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), a bike-a-thon that raises more money for charity than any other single athletic fundraising event in the world, has built an unparalleled track record for success strengthened by touchstone traditions and continuous improvements in pursuit of the goal of defying cancer.

Anchored in its storied past and animated by its hopeful future, the PMC made a record-breaking gift of $78 million to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, bringing the organization’s cumulative total to an astounding $1.125 billion raised since 1980. Powering this milestone contribution was the 46th annual PMC ride on Aug. 2-3, when 6,500 riders from 12 countries and 47 states pedaled 14 routes across Massachusetts. They were aided by 3,500 volunteers and 200 corporate sponsors, whose support ensured that 100% of every rider-raised dollar went directly to cancer research and care at Dana-Farber for the 19th consecutive year. 1,100 riders and volunteers were cancer survivors or current patients, considered Living Proof® of the PMC mission. Additionally, 160 Dana-Farber employees volunteered or rode, in some cases to fundraise for their own cancer research.

As Dana-Farber’s largest single contributor, representing 67% of the Jimmy Fund’s annual revenue, the PMC drives everything at Dana-Farber, accelerating breakthrough research to maximize innovation and progress while elevating essential care programs that support patients from diagnosis through survivorship. According to Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD, President and CEO at Dana-Farber and the Richard and Susan Smith Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, the PMC’s effect on Dana-Farber and its work is palpable and powerful. “Each day, we witness the profound impact of PMC funding,” he said, “We see it in new lifesaving treatments, in the determination of our researchers to make transformative discoveries, and in the ever-improving outcomes of our patients.”

“We ride to ensure that hope is never extinguished.”

Billy Starr, founder and chairman of the PMC, and Dana-Farber Trustee

A seven-year PMC rider, Ebert began his two-day trek at the Sturbridge Host Hotel, as have thousands of participants since 1981. 2025 marked Sturbridge’s final year as the PMC’s central Massachusetts starting line, which will move to the College of the Holy Cross in Worcester in 2026 to accommodate more participants, promote further growth, and provide more accessible and modern facilities. Susan Brogan, longtime Sturbridge coordinator with Matt McGuiness, reflected on the town’s indelible place in PMC history and Worcester’s potential to further elevate the ride. “Sturbridge really embraced the PMC, and what started here has impacted cancer worldwide,” said Brogan. “Our aim is to keep the needle moving forward, and Worcester provides an ideal opportunity for that.”

Billy Starr, founder and chairman of the PMC and a Dana-Farber Trustee, celebrated Sturbridge as “a cherished chapter in the PMC story” and underscored the importance of everyone’s continued commitment amid economic uncertainty and unprecedented cuts in federal research funding. “When others pull back this community accelerates,” Starr said. “We ride not just to raise money, but to support breakthroughs, ensure that hope is never extinguished, and make absolutely certain that nothing stands in the way of the cures we aspire to fund together.”

jetpack-related-posts.title: Back in the saddle again, 2022 PMC raises record $69 million—that’s $900 million since 1980!
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The world can always use more good news, so here is something great—the Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), the annual bike-a-thon that raises more money for charity than any other single athletic fundraising event in the country, had its best year yet, raising a record $69 million for Dana-Farber in 2022.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Pan-Mass Challenge raises record $72 million to bring cures closer by the mile
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On long journeys, landmarks and milestones show us where we are and how far we’ve come. Since 1980, the Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), the beloved bike-a-thon and the nation’s most successful athletic fundraiser, has seen plenty of both.

img.alt_text: Pan-Mass Challenge riders along the route

jetpack-related-posts.title: PMC Winter Cycle
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On Feb. 4, hundreds of riders assembled at Fenway Park’s 521 Overlook venue for the PMC Winter Cycle.

img.alt_text: Cyclists on stationary bikes at the 2023 PMC Winter Cycle

jetpack-related-posts.title: 2025 PMC Winter Cycle
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), the nation’s single most successful athletic fundraiser and Dana-Farber’s largest single contributor, kicked off its 2025 fundraising year at the 10th PMC Winter Cycle on Feb. 1 at Fenway Park.

img.alt_text: Bikers on stationary bikes at the PMC Winter Cycle event

jetpack-related-posts.title: One in a billion: Pan-Mass Challenge surpasses $1 billion fundraising milestone
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: In 2024, the Pan-Mass Challenge had a banner year, as the organization generated a record gift of $75 million and surpassed an extraordinary $1.047 billion in lifetime fundraising since its founding in 1980.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Wheeling in the years: The Pan-Mass Challenge produces origin story video
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: In 2024, to mark its 45th ride and to celebrate crossing a phenomenal $1 billion in lifetime fundraising, the PMC created a film bringing its origin story to life.

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Kathy Clute
Photography by Sam Ogden

How can exercise and diet improve the cognitive and physical abilities of cancer survivors 65 and older? Can artificial intelligence tools analyze clinical notes and other data in electronic medical records to determine which treatments are most effective?

Christina Dieli-Conwright, PhD, MPH, is a clinical exercise physiologist and the principal investigator (PI) in a 5-year collaboration with the University of Miami to determine whether older cancer survivors and their support persons can improve their cognitive and physical functioning through targeted lifestyle interventions.

Dieli-Conwright and her team are offering supervised and unsupervised home-based exercise and diet programs to 764 older cancer survivors and their primary caregivers, who are most often spouses or other family members. The participants are 65 or older and racially and ethnically diverse. One group will receive “gold standard” virtual aerobic and resistance exercise led by a certified trainer as well as virtual coaching by a registered dietician to promote adherence to a healthy Mediterranean diet that emphasizes fruits and vegetables, unsaturated fats, and less processed food.

The second group will be given the same diet recommendations and exercise intervention and equipment but will not receive the virtual coaching.

“There will be more than 26.1 million cancer survivors by 2040, and three quarters of them will be 65 or older—many with treatment-related side effects that affect their physical and cognitive functioning,” said Dieli-Conwright. “We also know that support persons tend to be less healthy than their peers who do not have caregiving responsibilities. We want to see which intervention we are testing is most successful in promoting a better quality of life for both populations.”

Kenneth Kehl, MD, MPH, is a thoracic oncologist and a researcher in Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s Division of Population Sciences. He is PI on a project to improve outcomes for patients by developing machine-learning techniques to extract data on disease progression, treatments, and outcomes from the electronic health records (EHRs) of more than 150,000 patients with advanced cancer. “This will make it possible to compare treatments that may be widely deployed but that don’t attract the resources necessary for randomized controlled trials,” said Kehl.

Both studies are supported by funding from the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute, a nonprofit organization with a mission to fund research designed to provide patients, caregivers, and clinicians with the evidence-based information they need to make better-informed health and health care decisions.

title.rendered: The Impact You Have Made Possible

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
Photography by John Deputy

Each year, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute aspires to provide the care and treatment our patients deserve. We are able to achieve these ambitions because of our dedicated donor community. In every issue of Impact, we share stories of generosity, and there are some accomplishments deserving of an honorable mention. We celebrate the impact you have made possible during 2025.

NEWLY NAMED FACULTY POSITIONS

In 2025, the following senior endowed positions were created or had new incumbents announced or installed, bringing our total number of senior endowed positions to 56.

LEADING THE WAY IN 2025 

  • Created an AI model to predict gene expression across human cells, advancing precision medicine. 
  • Introduced nursing-led research during Scholarship Week. 
  • Launched a first-of-its-kind lung cancer screening trial for never-smokers using a novel blood test. 
  • National Bureau of Economic Research reported that Dana-Farber has the highest scientific output per researcher of any institution in the world. 
  • Co-founded IGNITE, a first-ever consortium to eliminate health inequities in pediatric cancer care. 
  • Co-led a study of prostate cancer genetics in African populations to expand research in diverse groups. 
  • Advanced plans for a new cancer hospital through a bold clinical collaboration with BIDMC and HMFP. 
  • Opened a national-first simulation center to train oncology nurses in advanced ambulatory cancer care. 
  • Ranked among the best in pediatric cancer care nationally for the 18th straight year.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Expanding patient navigation through philanthropy
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: With donor support through The Dana-Farber Campaign, the Institute piloted a new community-facing patient navigation program in 2021 to assist patients with transportation, language services, insurance, nutrition, and other social and economic concerns that may be barriers to care.

img.alt_text: Patient Navigator Marlene Escobar and Vice President of Community Health Magnolia Contreras are pictured outside of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute

jetpack-related-posts.title: Unrestricted support: A powerful vote of confidence
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Dana-Farber Campaign is a catalyst for giving at every level, including through the Defy Cancer Fund, and has inspired tremendous unrestricted support from our generous philanthropic community.

img.alt_text: An image of a scientist looking through a test tube (image has blue overlay)

jetpack-related-posts.title: American Cancer Society grants propel research and programs forward
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The American Cancer Society (ACS) recently awarded more than $3.1 million in grants to 11 Dana-Farber Cancer Institute investigators. These grants support various areas across Dana-Farber, including research on improved outcomes and patient assistance programming to help with access to care.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Eisenson encourages CGAs as a simple and lasting legacy
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Supporting cancer research and care at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute can take many forms that benefit both the Institute and the donor. Michael Eisenson (pictured), Institute Trustee and chair of The Dana-Farber Campaign, recently established a charitable gift annuity (CGA) with a generous gift of $250,000.

img.alt_text: Michael Eisenson at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute's healing garden

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Dana-Farber Campaign
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Data science and AI allow us to better match patients to clinical trials, identify disparities in cancer care, and pinpoint the most promising treatment options.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Dana-Farber Campaign
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: One way our supporters accelerate campaign efforts is by including Dana-Farber in their estate plans.

title.rendered: Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon breaks records with $5.7 million raised for Dana-Farber

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Robbie Merritt and Nathalie Sczublewski
Photography by John Deputy, Matt Teuten

The WEEI/NESN Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon presented by Arbella Insurance continued to be a beacon of support for Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund in August with a record-breaking fundraising year. The inspirational two-day event, which has united our community since 2002, raised more than $5.7 million, bringing its lifetime total to $80 million in support of adult and pediatric cancer care and research at Dana-Farber.

The broadcast went live from Fenway Park Aug. 18 and 19 from 6 a.m. through midnight and featured stories of resilience and hope from patients, doctors, community leaders, and special guests. This year’s event made history, surpassing $5 million for the first time thanks to gifts from more than 15,000 donors across all 50 states. More than 70% of donations were under $100, showcasing the collective impact of grassroots generosity. A transformative $1 million match from longtime Dana-Farber supporters and philanthropists Rob and Karen Hale further inspired donors to make a difference.

The event included special appearances from Jimmy Fund Co-Chairs Tom Caron and Brock Holt; Jimmy Fund Captain and Red Sox pitcher Garrett Whitlock; Brianna Wakefield, daughter of the late Tim and Stacy Wakefield; Red Sox manager Alex Cora; Boston Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla; and Boston Bruins head coach Marco Sturm, among many others. Gayle O’Connell, executive vice president and chief marketing officer of Arbella Insurance, also appeared on the broadcast, reflecting on the longstanding partnership between Arbella and the Jimmy Fund and their decades of supporting the annual event.

“We’re thrilled to have raised a record-breaking $5.7 million to support adults and children with cancer,” said Jimmy Fund Co-Chairs Tom Caron and Brock Holt. “Together, we have made history, making a significant impact in the fight against cancer, and with continued support, we can lessen the burden of cancer for families. We are humbled and grateful for the tremendous outpouring of support from Red Sox Nation during the WEEI/NESN Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon presented by Arbella Insurance.”

jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: A longtime partner of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund, Arbella Insurance Group continued its steadfast support of Dana-Farber’s mission throughout 2023, living out the company’s motto of: “Here. For Good.”

jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The WEEI/NESN Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon presented by Arbella Insurance helped strike out cancer for the 22nd year at Fenway Park in August, raising nearly $4 million for adult and pediatric cancer care and research at Dana-Farber.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Arbella Insurance Foundation

jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Special thanks to our friends at Arbella Insurance Foundation, which is making a $50 contribution for each strikeout thrown by a Boston Red Sox pitcher up to $100,000 in total. title.rendered: American Cancer Society grants propel research and programs forward

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Cait Roberts

The American Cancer Society (ACS) recently awarded more than $3.1 million in grants to 11 Dana-Farber Cancer Institute investigators. These grants support various areas across Dana-Farber, including research on improved outcomes and patient assistance programming to help with access to care.

Supporting the next generation of researchers at Dana-Farber, Jennifer Mack, MD, MPH, received an institutional grant to develop a program for investigators to apply for seed grants, with three individuals funded annually to pursue their research.

A grant to support the work of Ann Partridge, MD, MPH, the Eric P. Winer, MD, Chair in Breast Cancer Research at Dana-Farber, will further her research into the treatment and care of adolescents and young adults with breast cancer who are more likely to suffer physically and emotionally after a diagnosis, compared with older patients. Partridge’s work aims to improve treatment outcomes and support quality of life for this population, as well as extend her impactful work to people with other types of young-onset breast cancer.

Focusing on treatments, Nilay Sethi, MD, PhD, was awarded a grant to aid in the development of new treatments that target the unique biology of colorectal cancer through a deeper review of factors related to the cancer’s shape-shifting behavior. Pere Puigserver, PhD, received a grant to help develop new strategies to enhance the efficacy of immunotherapeutic treatments for better patient outcomes.

The goal of grants received by Deborah Toffler, MSW, LCSW, and Christopher Lathan, MD, MS, MPH, the Christopher and Constance Hadley Family Chair at Dana-Farber, will help ensure Dana-Farber is accessible to all patients and families. Toffler’s grant will provide need-based lodging support to patients. Lathan’s grant will support Dana-Farber’s Community-Focused Patient Navigators to provide transportation for underserved patients.

“These scientists are on track to advance innovative cancer treatment, support, and care. We are excited to be a part of moving this work forward to help save lives.”

Christina Annunziata, MD, PhD, American Cancer Society

Building upon successful research on how to preserve healthy cells during cancer treatment, Olasunkanmi Olaoye, PhD, received funding to investigate a protein found to activate drugs specifically in tumors, helping to create safer treatments for patients.

Bringing comfort to patients, families, and Jimmy Fund Clinic team members is the professional responsibility of Opry, Dana-Farber’s first facility dog. Kate Nixon, CCLS, received a grant to support Opry’s work and efforts to provide tailored interventions for patients.

Other recent awardees include Yixiang Li, PhD; Sangwoo Park, PhD; and Sehyun Oh, PhD.

“The American Cancer Society is very proud to help fund these researchers and these critical areas of study,” said Christina Annunziata, MD, PhD, senior vice president, extramural discovery science at ACS. “These scientists are on track to advance innovative cancer treatment, support, and care. We are excited to be a part of moving this work forward to help save lives.”

title.rendered: Deitch’s formula for impact accelerates progress

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Amber Sinicrope
Photography by Celia D. Luna

Joseph S. Deitch, founder and Chairman Emeritus of Commonwealth Financial Network and creator of the Elevate Prize Foundation, is a philanthropist with a bold vision: to amplify changemakers and inspire collective action. He believes that empowering leaders in their fields can spark transformative change and redefine what’s possible.

Deitch’s recent $3 million gift to endow the Joseph Deitch Family Chair at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute exemplifies this vision. The chair, held by Eric Fischer, PhD, Director of the Chemical Biology Program at Dana-Farber, provides critical resources to fuel innovative cancer research. The decision to endow the chair was driven by Deitch’s trust in Dana-Farber’s leadership and his relationship with Laurie H. Glimcher, MD, President and CEO Emerita of Dana-Farber. “When Laurie told me this was one of her top priorities, that was enough for me,” Deitch recalled. “Then I met Eric. His brilliance, curiosity, and ability to unite diverse scientific disciplines made a powerful impression.”

Fischer’s pioneering work in targeted protein degradation—a therapeutic approach with wide-reaching potential—has positioned him as a leader in cancer biology. His research is reshaping drug development and transforming standards of care, offering promising alternatives to chemotherapy. Being named the inaugural incumbent of the Joseph Deitch Family Chair is an honor and a transformative opportunity for Fischer. “This recognition is not just for me, but for my entire lab and everyone who has contributed for more than a decade,” he said. “It’s also a vote of confidence in the future.”

The nature of the funding is especially critical, enabling Fischer and his team to take risks, test bold ideas, and unlock new directions. “Every dollar of flexible support can be multiplied tenfold in additional support,” Fischer reflected. “It accelerates everything—our speed, our reach, and ultimately, our impact on patients.”

“Philanthropy is deeply personal—find what speaks to you and act on it.”

Joseph S. Deitch

This remarkable gift builds on the $3 million Deitch contributed in 2023 to help launch the Centers for Early Detection and Interception and advance Dana-Farber’s Presidential Initiatives Fund. Deitch’s philanthropy also extends beyond Dana-Farber and cancer research. Through the Elevate Prize Foundation, he supports changemakers across disciplines while also empowering communities to create local solutions to global challenges.

Deitch’s giving centers on finding proven leaders with the vision and capacity to drive change—investing in their growth and amplifying their work to draw greater support. “I’m not someone who seeks the spotlight,” he said. “But I hope endowing this chair inspires others to think about how they can make a difference. Philanthropy is deeply personal—find what speaks to you and act on it.”

jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan

title.rendered: Family of Jane Rodgers honors her memory with new Dana-Farber chair

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Brittany Flaherty
Photography by Matt Teuten

When Jane Rodgers was diagnosed with cancer in 2019, her family took comfort in the fact that she was receiving the best possible care at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Jane’s natural ability to connect with people meant her doctors and nurses soon felt like an extension of the family.

“My mom was the kind of person everyone loved,” said Jane’s daughter, Ariana Rodgers. “She radiated kindness and warmth. She was creative and intelligent. She loved painting watercolors and quilting and listening to college lectures on quantum mechanics just for fun.”

After Jane passed away in 2020, her family knew they wanted to make a gift together in her honor to demonstrate their gratitude for her care and to help prevent other patients and families from experiencing such a devastating loss. Their $3 million gift established the Jane Rodgers Chair at Dana-Farber with David A. Barbie, MD, director of the Lowe Center for Thoracic Oncology, as the first incumbent. “Philanthropy was really important to my mom,” said Ariana. “She emphasized that to us throughout her life and really cared about medical research. She would be very proud of this gift that we’re making and excited for the future of this research.”

Jane’s five children—Ariana, Brooke Eanes, Jack Bishop, Joyce-Ann Bishop, and Virginia Ermentrout—came together to make this special gift alongside Jane’s husband, Ronald Rodgers, through the MacDonald Family Foundation. The Jane Rodgers Chair will enable Barbie to further his thoracic oncology and immunotherapy research in perpetuity, with the goal of transforming care for patients with this challenging disease.

“I am truly honored by the incredibly generous support of the Jane Rodgers Family to carry on her legacy as we work to transform care for patients with lung cancer,” said Barbie. “This support will speed our efforts to expand treatment options, and we are grateful for the family’s meaningful partnership.”

Barbie is widely recognized for his pioneering work in the field of lung cancer, having led groundbreaking translational research that has expanded treatment options for patients, including those with KRAS-driven cancers previously considered undruggable. Ariana noted that persistent stigmas around lung cancer mean it doesn’t attract as much research support as other, less deadly diseases. Learning this confirmed her family’s decision to honor their mother’s memory and the compassionate team that had given her their time and care.

“The doctors are what set Dana-Farber apart. They’re passionate, knowledgeable, and we always felt heard and supported,” said Ariana, sharing that one of her mother’s nurses went out of her way to find her mom her favorite drink: Mexican Coca-Cola in a glass bottle. “It made my mom’s day, that special touch. Dana-Farber is incredible.”

title.rendered: Advancing Parkinson’s research: Spiegelman’s groundbreaking work

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah
Photography by Sam Ogden

From a remarkable act of generosity, the Tyler Family has donated $3 million to establish the Tyler Family Fund for Parkinson’s Research, supporting the groundbreaking work of Bruce Spiegelman, PhD, the Stanley J. Korsmeyer, MD, Professor of Cell Biology and Medicine at Harvard Medical School. This gift is a testament to their commitment to advancing research that could change the lives of millions affected by Parkinson’s Disease (PD), a condition that has personally impacted their family.

Spiegelman, a renowned leader in cancer biology and metabolism, has dedicated his career to exploring the molecular mechanisms underlying various diseases. His research, while primarily focused on cancer, often yields insights into other human diseases, including PD. Spiegelman’s innovative approach to understanding the molecular benefits of exercise has led to significant discoveries, particularly the identification of irisin, a protein with very significant therapeutic potential.

“Exercise and other forms of physical activity have been shown to markedly lower the incidence of PD and slow its progression,” Spiegelman explained. “Our goal is not to replace exercise but to use it as a platform for discovering new molecules that can be used as therapeutics for PD.”

Spiegelman’s lab was the first in the world to identify irisin, a protein linked to exercise, in 2012. Since then, they have demonstrated its striking effects in cellular and animal models of Alzheimer’s Disease and Parkinson’s Disease. In PD, the accumulation of toxic proteins like α-synuclein in neurons leads to motor symptoms. Irisin has shown promise in blocking this accumulation and preserving motor function in animal models.

“We are optimistic about the impact this research could have on stopping and perhaps reversing disease symptoms.”

Bruce Spiegelman, PhD

The Tyler Family Fund will enable Dr. Spiegelman’s team to accelerate their research, focusing on engineering irisin for therapeutic use. “This funding is absolutely crucial,” Spiegelman said. “It allows us to advance the study of irisin toward clinical trials, potentially offering a breakthrough treatment for PD. We are optimistic about the impact this research could have on stopping and perhaps even reversing disease symptoms.”

The Tyler Family’s gift offers new hope for those affected by PD. By supporting Spiegelman’s pioneering work, they are investing in a future where the disease and perhaps other neurological disorders can be effectively managed, and potentially even reversed. Their generosity underscores the importance of funding exploratory research that holds the promise of transformative breakthroughs.

jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Margaret and Michael Kerr’s generous gift of $100,000 to the Kerr Family Fund for Translational Research supports the groundbreaking work of James Cleary, MD, PhD, at Dana-Farber. title.rendered: Dolores Tassinari’s gift supports Hodgkin lymphoma care and research

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

When Dolores Tassinari passed away at the age of 94 last year, she left behind a legacy of quiet strength, family devotion, and enduring generosity. A longtime resident of Plymouth, Mass., Dolores lived a life rooted in service—to her family, her community, and, in her final wishes, to a cause deeply personal to her heart.

In 2025, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute received an extraordinary estate gift of $2,464,652 from the Dolores E. Tassinari estate. Designated to support research and treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma, the gift honors the memory of Dolores’ beloved daughter, Suzanne Tassinari, who died of the illness in 1991.

For over four decades, Dolores worked alongside her husband, Ernest, as a public accountant in Plymouth. She was a woman of many passions, finding joy in gardening, reading, and cheering on the Red Sox. Dolores cherished weekly Scrabble games with her neighbors and took pride in her role as a mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother.

Her generous bequest to Dana-Farber reflects her enduring love for Suzanne and her desire to help others facing a similar diagnosis. It will help accelerate the work of Dana-Farber’s clinicians and scientists as they pursue new therapies and improved outcomes for patients with Hodgkin lymphoma.

“My parents understood that Dana-Farber was the institution with the deepest and broadest set of skills and experience in New England for cancer treatment and research.”

Mark Tassinari

Dolores’ legacy centers around her children, and she is survived by her daughter Marie Bower of Maryland, sons Edward Tassinari of Plymouth, and Mark Tassinari of Pembroke, New Hampshire—as well as five grandchildren and six great-grandchildren. Her gift ensures that her family’s story will continue to touch the lives of countless others.

“My parents understood that Dana-Farber was the institution with the deepest and broadest set of skills and experience in New England for cancer treatment and research,” said Mark.

“My sister’s condition ultimately proved incurable with the medical resources and treatments available in 1990 and 1991. It was my mother’s wish, and indeed that of our entire family, to contribute to the ongoing efforts at Dana-Farber to find new and effective treatments for the benefit of others.”

Dolores’ legacy, like the garden she so lovingly tended, will continue to grow—bringing hope to patients and families for generations to come.

title.rendered: Suprenant’s intuitive philanthropy drives holistic cancer care

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Lucy McDonald

Cynthia Suprenant believes in keeping things simple. While her cumulative $1 million in contributions across Dana-Farber Cancer Institute may seem driven by results or carefully calculated outcomes, she insists her approach is rooted in something far more intuitive. Much like an investor backing promising startups, Suprenant places her trust in the leadership and vision of the institutions she supports, believing they are best equipped to identify where resources can make the greatest impact.

Suprenant traces her philosophy of giving back to her childhood, inspired by her Grandma Sullivan, who would carefully budget her household expenses and still set aside small amounts to give back to the local church. That early example of quiet generosity left a lasting impression on Suprenant, shaping her approach to philanthropy as an act of planting seeds and trusting experts to nurture them into something extraordinary. “I trust that the Institute will tell me what it needs,” Suprenant explained. “I just want to help smart people do things for sick people. I don’t want anything back from Dana-Farber other than for the good work to continue.” It was this same spirit of giving that guided her to Dana-Farber in 2017.

In addition to supporting Dana-Farber’s Institute priorities through unrestricted funding, Suprenant has focused her philanthropy on two key areas: the Program for Older Adults with Breast Cancer and the Leonard P. Zakim Center for Integrative Therapies and Healthy Living. Both reflect her intuitive approach to philanthropy, addressing needs that may not always be central to traditional cancer care but are deeply impactful for patients.

“I just want to help smart people do things for sick people.”

Cynthia Suprenant

The Program for Older Adults with Breast Cancer, one of the first of its kind in the U.S., serves patients over 70 by addressing their unique concerns. It offers specialized care, nutritional support, social workers, financial assistance, and integrative therapies. This multidisciplinary approach ensures patients receive holistic care to improve their quality of life. “A 78-year-old’s experience with recurrence is completely different from a 47-year-old’s,” Suprenant said. Her support has helped expand personalized care, empowering older patients with their treatment options.

The Leonard P. Zakim Center for Integrative Therapies and Healthy Living offerings align with Suprenant’s belief in holistic care. For 25 years, the center has complemented medical treatment with therapies that reduce pain, anxiety, and side effects while improving quality of life. With support from donors like Suprenant, the center has expanded its offerings, helping patients navigate their cancer journeys.

Through $1 million in contributions, Suprenant has shown philanthropy doesn’t need a formula. Guided by intuition and trust, her giving supports meaningful care, whether for older adults with breast cancer or integrative therapies and highlights the impact of thoughtful, heartfelt philanthropy.

excerpt.rendered: Cynthia Suprenant believes in keeping things simple. While her cumulative $1 million in contributions across Dana-Farber Cancer Institute may seem driven by results or carefully calculated outcomes, she insists her approach is rooted in something far more intuitive. Much like an investor backing promising startups, Suprenant places her trust in the leadership and vision of the institutions she supports, believing they are best equipped to identify where resources can make the greatest impact.

title.rendered: Kicks for Cancer harnesses power of community to drive cancer research

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Caitlin Henault
Photography by Henry Morgan

Nearly 20 years ago, Concord-Carlisle High School hosted its first Kicks for Cancer soccer match to honor the memory of Lois Wells, the mother of assistant men’s soccer coach Steve Wells, who passed away from ovarian cancer. Today, Kicks for Cancer has grown into a vibrant week-long celebration that unites the community in a shared mission to honor loved ones impacted by cancer while supporting groundbreaking cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

Anchored by its signature soccer tournament, which features 16 back-to-back matches between teams from surrounding towns in a single day, Kicks for Cancer has expanded to include a variety of sports, arts, and music, creating opportunities for all students to take part. In 2024, Kicks for Cancer reached a significant milestone, raising over $1 million to support Dana-Farber.

“Nearly everyone in our community can tell a story about someone in their life who has been affected by cancer,” said Trish Siefer, Kicks for Cancer’s event chair. “Kicks for Cancer unifies Concord-Carlisle—it gives us all a chance to honor survivors, remember those we have lost, and rally to support lifesaving research.”

Funds raised by Kicks for Cancer support ovarian cancer early detection and prevention research led by Dipanjan Chowdhury, PhD, the Svanberg Family Chair at Dana-Farber, largely due to the advocacy of beloved community member Jenna Swaim, who passed away in 2018. Because there are currently no established screening or detection methods for ovarian cancer, it is often discovered in later stages when treatment options are more limited. Chowdhury is leading efforts to advance a promising blood test for ovarian cancer that examines microRNAs, tiny molecules in the blood that may serve as early biomarkers for the disease—helping to predict if women at high genetic risk of ovarian cancer are likely to develop the disease.

“The ability to detect ovarian cancer early will greatly enhance our ability to treat patients effectively and provide them with hope for long-term survival,” said Chowdhury. “Kicks for Cancer is fueling research that has the potential to save countless lives, demonstrating the power of community to drive meaningful progress in cancer research.”

In September, 32 soccer teams took the field for Kicks for Cancer’s 19th season, proudly wearing the event’s signature pink and teal jerseys adorned with the names of loved ones.

“Our dream is to help people detect their cancer early, because if it can be caught sooner, women like Lois and Jenna might still be here,” said Trish. “This event is so important to us, and this research will help prevent us from losing another member of our community too soon.”

excerpt.rendered: Nearly 20 years ago, Concord-Carlisle High School hosted its first Kicks for Cancer soccer match to honor the memory of Lois Wells, the mother of assistant men’s soccer coach Steve Wells, who passed away from ovarian cancer. Today, Kicks for Cancer has grown into a vibrant week-long celebration that unites the community in a shared mission to honor loved ones impacted by cancer while supporting groundbreaking cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Kicks for Cancer celebrates record-setting year
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Each year since 2007, Kicks for Cancer has brought together athletes and fans from Concord-Carlisle High School and 17 surrounding towns to raise funds for ovarian cancer research at Dana-Farber.

img.alt_text: Young soccer players in bright pink shirts

jetpack-related-posts.title: Kicks for Cancer
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Each September, the Concord-Carlisle High School community in Concord, Mass., comes together for Kicks for Cancer, an opportunity for area high school sports teams to support Dr.  Dipanjan Chowdhury's Ovarian Cancer Early Detection Fund. The 2022 event raised $116,000 for Dana-Farber and honored students’ loved ones who have faced cancer.

img.alt_text: Two soccer players at the Kicks for Cancer event

jetpack-related-posts.title: Minnesota Ovarian Cancer Alliance
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Ovarian cancer is often difficult to treat at later stages and difficult to detect at earlier stages. With a $100,000 grant, the Minnesota Ovarian Cancer Alliance is supporting research at Dana-Farber into the development of an ultrasensitive blood test to detect ovarian cancer at its earliest, and most treatable, stages.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Krafts champion early detection and prevention for at-risk communities
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: With a gift of $5 million to The Dana-Farber Campaign, the Kraft Family will bring Dana-Farber’s lifesaving early detection and prevention programs to more people at risk of developing cancer.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Tina’s Wish
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Longtime supporter Tina’s Wish recently awarded more than $450,000 over a two-year period to support two Dana-Farber studies into early detection for ovarian cancer—one investigating a new class of microRNA and key biomarkers and how they could be used to develop a personalized blood test, and another examining how epigenetic…

jetpack-related-posts.title: V is for victory over intractable cancers
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The V Foundation for Cancer Research, founded by legendary basketball coach Jim Valvano, has granted $1.6 million to four Dana-Farber investigators.

title.rendered: A legacy of care: Elevating palliative nursing education

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Kayla Carcone

When Shannon Robins reflects on her mother’s legacy, she sees a lifelong commitment to nursing, education, and compassionate care. Jean Cunningham, a nurse for over 40 years, worked her way from a staff nurse to an executive role in nursing, all while earning advanced degrees and raising her family. Even as she fought breast cancer for over a decade, Jean’s dedication to her profession and her patients never wavered.

“My mother was a lifelong nurse who worked tirelessly to educate and empower others,” Shannon shared. “Supporting this program is my way of carrying on what she started.” Shannon and her husband, Jason Robins, co-founder and CEO of DraftKings, a Jimmy Fund corporate sponsor, made a visionary $1 million gift to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, helping to launch a first-of-its-kind palliative care education program designed by nurses, for nurses. The first cohort begins this fall. The initiative aims to train 100% of Dana-Farber’s nursing staff in palliative care, ensuring that every patient—regardless of their stage of cancer—has access to supportive care that addresses their physical, emotional, and spiritual needs.

“Palliative care isn’t just about the end of someone’s life—it’s about improving quality of living at every stage of the journey.”

Shannon Robins

Palliative care is specialized medical care focused on relieving the symptoms, side effects, and stress of serious illness—helping patients maintain the best possible quality of life throughout treatment. “Palliative care isn’t just about the end of someone’s life—it’s about improving quality of living at every stage of the journey,” Shannon explained.

Vanessa Battista, Senior Nursing Director of Palliative Care, emphasized the program’s transformative potential. “This initiative is about empowering nurses to provide compassionate, patient-centered care during some of the most complex moments in oncology,” she said. “It’s a cultural shift that aligns with Dana-Farber’s commitment to total patient care.”

The program also reflects a broader movement to elevate the role of nurses in oncology. Nurses are often the first point of contact for patients and families, fielding difficult questions and providing critical support. Shannon hopes the program will give nurses the confidence and tools they need to navigate these moments with ease.

With Dana-Farber’s new dedicated inpatient cancer hospital and the future clinical collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, a Harvard-affiliated academic medical center, and its physician group, Harvard Medical Faculty Physicians, the program’s impact is poised to grow. Hundreds of new nurses will join Dana-Farber in the coming years, and Shannon envisions this training becoming a model for other healthcare organizations.

“My hope is that palliative care becomes a standard part of every patient’s experience,” Shannon said. “This gift is about honoring my mother’s legacy, but it’s also to ensure that every family feels supported during their experience.”

excerpt.rendered: Shannon Robins and her husband, Jason Robins, co-founder and CEO of DraftKings, a Jimmy Fund corporate sponsor, made a visionary $1 million gift to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, helping to launch a first-of-its-kind palliative care education program designed by nurses, for nurses.

title.rendered: Trustee Science Committee fosters the next generation of researchers

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Cyrena Musset
Photography by Michael Blanchard

Shelby Roseman, PhD, and Amanda Smythers, PhD, were recently named the latest group of Trustee Science Committee Postdoctoral Fellows at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. The fellowship was launched in 2020 with donations from the Trustee Science Committee (TSC), a group of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute board members responsible for advancing research and cultivating scientific talent at all levels at Dana-Farber. Since the program’s inception, the TSC has raised more than $1 million to foster the next generation of cancer researchers.

Roseman is working to establish a collaborative research group to explore how epigenetic mechanisms drive cancer progression and drug resistance. Her work investigates the role of dysregulated repetitive DNA sequences, often dismissed as “junk DNA,” in shaping cancer cell states. By deepening our understanding of gene regulation in cancer, she aims to contribute to the development of innovative therapies. Roseman is currently conducting her research in the lab of Bradley Bernstein, MD, PhD, the Richard and Nancy Lubin Family Chair at Dana-Farber, a leader in epigenomics. Under Bernstein’s mentorship, she is building the foundation for her long-term goal of becoming a professor and advancing research on epigenetic regulation in cancer.

Smythers is driven by a deep passion for the scientific process and aspires to lead her own research group as a principal investigator (PI). Her scientific journey began with foundational research on topics ranging from photosynthetic electron transfer to tardigrade biology. As a postdoctoral fellow, she is integrating her background in fundamental science with translational research to address questions that can improve patient outcomes. Smythers is co-advised by Steve Gygi, PhD, at Harvard Medical School, and Bruce Spiegelman, PhD, who is the Stanley J. Korsmeyer, MD, Professor of Cell Biology and Medicine at Harvard Medical School, and Edward Chouchani, PhD, at Dana-Farber. Her primary work in the Spiegelman Lab focuses on applying her expertise in analytical chemistry to critical biological questions, while her involvement in the Gygi Lab allows her to advance mass spectrometry techniques. In the Chouchani Lab, she combines method development with biological implementation. This multidisciplinary training positions her to mentor the next generation of scientists while pursuing impactful research as a future PI.

“The Trustee Science Committee Fellowship plays a critical role in empowering individuals to pursue their passions and contribute to the future of science.”

Levi Garraway, MD, PhD, Dana-Farber Trustee

“Scientists come from all backgrounds, and their diverse perspectives drive innovation and discovery,” said Dana-Farber Trustee Levi Garraway, MD, PhD. “Supporting early career researchers is essential to ensure talent isn’t lost due to lack of resources. I give to the Trustee Science Committee Fellowship because it plays a critical role in empowering these individuals to pursue their passions and contribute to the future of science.”

jetpack-related-posts.title: Levi Garraway
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Dana-Farber Trustee Levi Garraway, MD, PhD, has supported the Trustee Science Committee Fellowships with a generous $250,000 gift—adding a third year to the fellowship. Created to advance the research and cultivate the talent of scientists at all levels, this gift will further support fellows who are committed to finding new…

jetpack-related-posts.title: Phyllis and Richard Krock
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Institute Trustee Phyllis Krock and her husband, Richard, gave a generous gift of $100,000 to the Palm Beach Initiative. The funds are dedicated to the Presidential Initiatives Fund under Dana-Farber President and CEO Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD. With this support, Dana-Farber physicians and researchers can continue developing innovative cancer…

jetpack-related-posts.title: NYC reception spotlights future of research and care
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Dana-Farber Trustees, Pan-Mass Challenge Heavy Hitters, supporters, and friends gathered at Cure in New York City to meet Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD, and engage in conversation about the path forward for Dana-Farber.

img.alt_text: Three people speaking at an event on stage

jetpack-related-posts.title: Dolecki Family gives back to advance pediatric cancer therapies
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: When Charlotte Dolecki passed away, she had a provision in her trust for charity. The trustee—her great-nephew, Vincent Dello-Iacono—and her great-niece, Danielle Comella, immediately knew where they wanted to make a gift.

img.alt_text: The Dolecki Family presents a ceremonial check to Lisa Scherber, director of patient and family programs in the Jimmy Fund Clinic, and Scott Armstrong, MD, PhD.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Cox Family continues support of Dana-Farber’s revolutionary science
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Career venture capitalist and Institute Trustee Howard Cox and his wife, Wendy Cox, are no strangers to the revolutionary science and clinical treatments happening at the Institute.

jetpack-related-posts.title: American Cancer Society grants propel research and programs forward
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The American Cancer Society (ACS) recently awarded more than $3.1 million in grants to 11 Dana-Farber Cancer Institute investigators. These grants support various areas across Dana-Farber, including research on improved outcomes and patient assistance programming to help with access to care.

title.rendered: A record-breaking year for Dana-Farber’s ASICS Falmouth Road Race team

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Sofi Elbadawi
Photography by Fidelis Teixeira

The ASICS Falmouth Road Race, a scenic seven-mile race along the Cape Cod coast, is one of the most well-known summer running events in New England, with race bibs highly sought after by runners from all over the globe. Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund is the official Legacy Partner of the Numbers for Nonprofits Program, the charity arm of the Falmouth Road Race. This year, on August 17, runners from Dana-Farber’s 2025 Falmouth Road Race team raised a record-breaking $1,105,554.90, the highest fundraising total in the team’s 23-year history, which exceeds $12.5 million to date for innovative research and compassionate patient care. The 2025 team also set a recruitment record, with 366 runners forming Dana-Farber’s largest Falmouth team yet. For many of these runners, the race was more than just a reason to lace up their sneakers—it was personal.

“I was diagnosed with invasive breast cancer in October 2023,” shared Catie Smith, a member of this year’s team. “Over the past 18 months, I’ve experienced firsthand how important the research and care options at Dana-Farber are, especially for patients like me,” she reflected.

Catie first ran the Falmouth Road Race 20 years ago. When the opportunity arose to run the seven-mile race again, this time in support of Dana-Farber, she didn’t hesitate.

“It was a no-brainer,” she said. “Everyone deserves access to high quality, research-based care. I hope that by running, I am doing my small part to advance the options available to future cancer patients.”

For others, like Trey Witter, the race was a way to honor loved ones who have benefited from Dana-Farber’s care. Trey ran this year’s Falmouth Road Race in honor of his father, who was diagnosed with leukemia.

“My dad would not be here if it wasn’t for the treatment he received at Dana-Farber.” Trey shared. “I’m honored to pay it forward to the doctors, nurses, and patients like my dad by running for Dana-Farber’s team.”

2025 also marked an incredible 20th consecutive Falmouth Road Race for Team Lanzoni/Bergeron founder Jim Kiley. Back in 2006, Jim was motivated to run with Dana-Farber after his friend David passed away from cancer. What started as a team of one has become a 20-year legacy, with hundreds of team members joining and thousands of dollars raised to support Dana-Farber’s lifesaving mission. When asked what keeps him coming back to the race year after year, Jim didn’t hesitate to share: “I do it for the doctors and patients at Dana-Farber. It’s that simple.”

jetpack-related-posts.title: Dana-Farber team defies cancer in ASICS Falmouth Road Race
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On Aug. 21, more than 330 members of Dana-Farber’s team ran seven miles along the scenic Cape Cod coastline for the 50th running of the ASICS Falmouth Road Race.

img.alt_text: Falmouth Road Race Team Power runners

jetpack-related-posts.title: Falmouth Road Race team surpasses $10 million milestone
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On August 20, more than 325 participants laced up on behalf of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to compete in the ASICS Falmouth Road Race.

img.alt_text: A Falmouth Road Race runner poses for a photo

jetpack-related-posts.title: Falmouth Road Race: Pacing the way forward against cancer
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On August 18, 352 runners ran the scenic ASICS Falmouth Road Race for Dana-Farber, raising nearly $1 million for cancer research and patient care.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Jimmy Fund celebrates 75 years
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On May 22, 1948, Einar Gustafson, a young boy being treated for lymphoma by Dr. Sidney Farber and dubbed “Jimmy” to protect his privacy, shared his story from his hospital bed.

img.alt_text: The original Jimmy in a hospital bed with an old TV

jetpack-related-posts.title: Dana-Farber’s Boston half team sets new record
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Sunday, November 9, marked the Boston Athletic Association’s (B.A.A.’s) annual Boston Half, a scenic 13.1-mile race through Franklin Park and the Emerald Necklace Park System.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Dana-Farber recruits largest B.A.A. Half Marathon® team to date
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The 2023 B.A.A. Half Marathon® was a race to remember, with 650 participants running Sunday, Nov. 12, to support Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s race toward a cancer-free future.

img.alt_text: A group photo of Dana-Farber runners at the BAA Half Marathon in 2023

title.rendered: Dana-Farber researchers awarded American Society of Hematology funding

content.rendered:
Winter 2025 
By Elyse Pleickhardt 

The American Society of Hematology (ASH) funds groundbreaking research on blood and bone marrow disorders. Over the past year, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers have earned a total of $845,000 in competitive ASH grants. 

Each Junior Faculty Scholar Award winner was granted $150,000. Recipient Roger Belizaire, MD, PhD, will continue to bridge gaps in the understanding of VEXAS syndrome, an inflammatory disorder that causes blood cell abnormalities. Zuzana Tothova, MD, PhD, aims to advance our understanding of blood cancer development in patients with inherited mutations in the gene RUNX1. Reid Merryman, MD, will continue to research immunotherapies for follicular lymphoma as alternatives to current, more toxic treatments. Additional ASH awards were granted to:  

  • Erin Parry, MD, PhD – 2024 Basic/Translational Fellow to Faculty Scholar Award: $125,000 
  • Nicoletta Cieri, MD, PhD – 2024 Basic/Translational Research Fellow Scholar Award: $100,000
  • Frederick Tsai, MD, PhD – 2024 Research Training Award for Fellows: $70,000
  • Miriam Osei, MD, MPH – 2025 Hematology Inclusion Pathway Fellow Award: $100,000 

“ASH is proud to recognize the work of Dana-Farber grantees and their innovative efforts to improve the lives of present and future blood cancer patients around the world,” said Belinda Avalos, MD, ASH president. We look forward to seeing the lifesaving impact of Dana-Farber ASH grantees’ dedicated research in the coming years.

title.rendered: Stephen B. Farber & Deirdre E. Curley make $1 million gift to honor family legacy

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Longtime Dana-Farber Cancer Institute supporters Trustee Stephen B. Farber and his wife Deirdre E. Curley made a $1 million gift to the Ellen Farber Schmidt Fund, which provides unrestricted support to Dana-Farber. The gift honors the memory of Steve’s sister, Ellen, who passed away in 2024, and continues the family’s legacy at Dana-Farber. Steve and Dee established the fund in 2024 with an initial gift of $250,000.

Steve is the son of Dr. Sidney Farber, who founded the Children’s Cancer Research Foundation (now Dana-Farber) in 1947 and is widely regarded as the father of modern chemotherapy. Steve joined the Board of Trustees in 1973 and is currently its longest-serving member. For 52 years, Steve and Dee have strongly supported presidential initiatives, capital campaigns, endowed chairs, and other Dana-Farber priorities.

Their professional lives have focused on public service. After completing studies at Harvard and Princeton, Steve worked to improve U.S. fiscal and intergovernmental policies and operations, starting with the new anti-poverty programs of the 1960s. He was an adviser to Indiana Congressman John Brademas, New Jersey Governor Richard J. Hughes, and Harvard University President Derek Bok. He then served as executive director of the National Governors’ Association; chairman of Concordia Group, a national advisory service on fiscal and intergovernmental affairs; and chief adviser for the County Council of Montgomery County, Maryland. Dee, a Wellesley College graduate, worked for the U.S. Bureau of Consumer Protection, the Massachusetts Council on Crime and Correction, and Wisconsin Governor Patrick J. Lucey as the state’s director of intergovernmental relations. She then served as the chief analyst for fiscal and trade issues at the National Governors’ Association, where she and Steve met, and as Assistant Director of the U.S. Trade and Development Agency.

“My father lives on at Dana-Farber, just as he does in us,” Steve said. “This conviction is what animates the gifts Dee and I have made over the years. We are proud to support many vitally important organizations. Dana-Farber is and always will be foremost among them.”

“While some of our past gifts have been for specific purposes, we understand the value and importance of unrestricted gifts. The overriding goal is to maximize support of all kinds in order to build on Dana-Farber’s extraordinary achievements over more than three quarters of a century.”

Steve Farber and Dee Curley

Steve and Dee added: “While some of our past gifts have been for specific purposes, we understand the value and importance of unrestricted gifts. The overriding goal is to maximize support of all kinds in order to build on Dana-Farber’s extraordinary achievements over more than three quarters of a century.”

jetpack-related-posts.title: Stephen B. Farber & Deirdre E. Curley make $1 million gift
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Steve is the son of Dr. Sidney Farber, who founded the Children’s Cancer Research Foundation (now Dana-Farber) in 1947 and is widely regarded as the father of modern chemotherapy.

img.alt_text: Dr. Sidney Farber with a young patient

jetpack-related-posts.title: Dana-Farber Society reaches 2,000 members
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Dana-Farber Society honor those who have made a legacy gift, helping to secure future progress for Dana-Farber research and care.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Dana-Farber Society
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Dana-Farber Society (DFS) is a group of visionary donors who are changing lives and creating a legacy through a planned gift such as a bequest, life income gift, or beneficiary designation to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, the Jimmy Fund, the Friends of Dana-Farber, or the Pan-Mass Challenge.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Over $1 million raised from 2023 Palm Beach Annual Appeal
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Each year, the Palm Beach community generously comes together to raise funds for Dana-Farber.

img.alt_text: Phyllis and Richard Krock at the Palm Beach Annual Appeal

jetpack-related-posts.title: Eisenson encourages CGAs as a simple and lasting legacy
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Supporting cancer research and care at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute can take many forms that benefit both the Institute and the donor. Michael Eisenson (pictured), Institute Trustee and chair of The Dana-Farber Campaign, recently established a charitable gift annuity (CGA) with a generous gift of $250,000.

img.alt_text: Michael Eisenson at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute's healing garden

jetpack-related-posts.title: Phyllis and Richard Krock
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Institute Trustee Phyllis Krock and her husband, Richard, gave a generous gift of $100,000 to the Palm Beach Initiative. The funds are dedicated to the Presidential Initiatives Fund under Dana-Farber President and CEO Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD. With this support, Dana-Farber physicians and researchers can continue developing innovative cancer…

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
Photography by David Shopper

After more than a decade at the helm of Philanthropy Communications at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Assistant Vice President, Joyce Gallagher is embarking on her retirement journey.

Joyce joined the Division of Philanthropy at Dana-Farber in 2014, with over 35 years of communications and development experience—and a heart for the Dana-Farber mission. During her time here, she has led the Impact team, as well as the media relations and creative content teams. Joyce has seen us through more than 50 issues of Impact and its redesign, the Dana-Farber Campaign, the I Am Jimmy campaign, and countless Dana-Farber and Jimmy Fund features in the media. As a result, Dana-Farber has won numerous awards, including a 2025 AAMC Gold Award in Publications for Impact, and an international 2025 Gold Telly for a stellar Dana-Farber Campaign Close Video. In retirement, Joyce plans to consult and spend more time with her family. We salute Joyce for making a lasting impact and wish her an enjoyable and fulfilling next chapter!

jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Dana-Farber Society honor those who have made a legacy gift, helping to secure future progress for Dana-Farber research and care.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Expanding patient navigation through philanthropy
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: With donor support through The Dana-Farber Campaign, the Institute piloted a new community-facing patient navigation program in 2021 to assist patients with transportation, language services, insurance, nutrition, and other social and economic concerns that may be barriers to care.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Suprenant’s intuitive philanthropy drives holistic cancer care
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Cynthia Suprenant believes in keeping things simple. While her cumulative $1 million in contributions across Dana-Farber Cancer Institute may seem driven by results or carefully calculated outcomes, she insists her approach is rooted in something far more intuitive. Much like an investor backing promising startups, Suprenant places her trust in…

img.alt_text: Cynthia Suprenant in her garden with her bicycle and golden retriever

jetpack-related-posts.title: A Message from Melany Duval
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Dear friends, Every day our philanthropic community supports a relentless commitment to possibilities in cancer care at Dana-Farber—and that gives me hope.

jetpack-related-posts.title: A Message from Melany Duval
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Because of your support for The Dana-Farber Campaign, our impact and growth will expand by an order of magnitude we have only begun to imagine.

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah
Photography by John Deputy

The Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC) community came together at Rochambeau Restaurant in Boston on Sunday, Nov. 2, for the 2025 PMC Check Presentation. The annual event held by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s largest donor celebrated the extraordinary efforts of riders, volunteers, and donors, with 100% of every rider-raised dollar supporting Dana-Farber. Guests enjoyed brunch and drinks while sharing in the honor and excitement of unveiling the 2025 gift—a record-breaking total of $78 million raised through PMC weekend, PMC Unpaved, PMC Winter Cycle, and PMC Kids Rides.

Pictured:
Admiral Francis X. McDonald, LPD, Rear Admiral, USMS, President of Mass Maritime Academy 
Benjamin Ebert, President and CEO, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute 
Josh Bekenstein, Chair, Board of Trustees, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute 
Jarrett Collins, CEO, Pan-Mass Challenge 
Lisa Hughes, News Anchor, WBZ-TV 
Billy Starr, Founder and Chairman, Pan-Mass Challenge 
Meredith Beaton Starr, Director of Stewardship and Liaison to Dana-Farber, Pan-Mass Challenge 
Melany Duval, Senior Vice President, Chief Philanthropy Officer, The Jimmy Fund 
Mike Ascione, Chairman, Pan-Mass Challenge Board of Directors 
Chris Kay, Head of Enterprise Platforms, M&T Bank

jetpack-related-posts.title: Pan-Mass Challenge celebrates PMC Pedal Partners from the Jimmy Fund Clinic at Fenway Park
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On May 17, dozens of PMC Pedal Partners—pediatric patients from the Jimmy Fund Clinic at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute paired with PMC riders and teams—gathered at The 521 Overlook at Fenway Park to meet the cyclists participating in the 46th PMC on Aug. 2 and 3.

img.alt_text: A family of four at Fenway Park

jetpack-related-posts.title: 2025 PMC Winter Cycle
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), the nation’s single most successful athletic fundraiser and Dana-Farber’s largest single contributor, kicked off its 2025 fundraising year at the 10th PMC Winter Cycle on Feb. 1 at Fenway Park.

img.alt_text: Bikers on stationary bikes at the PMC Winter Cycle event

jetpack-related-posts.title: PMC Winter Cycle
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The one-of-a-kind PMC Winter Cycle was held at Fenway Park on March 9, with hundreds of riders participating to support patient care and research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

img.alt_text: Cyclists participating in the PMC Winter Cycle at Fenway Park

jetpack-related-posts.title: Celebrating the PMC’s $1 billion milestone
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: In January, Dana-Farber leadership welcomed dedicated members of the Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC) community for a special event celebrating their success raising more than $1 billion since 1980 and the transformative impact these funds have had on the lives of our patients.

jetpack-related-posts.title: One in a billion: Pan-Mass Challenge surpasses $1 billion fundraising milestone
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: In 2024, the Pan-Mass Challenge had a banner year, as the organization generated a record gift of $75 million and surpassed an extraordinary $1.047 billion in lifetime fundraising since its founding in 1980.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Pan-Mass Challenge raises record $72 million to bring cures closer by the mile
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On long journeys, landmarks and milestones show us where we are and how far we’ve come. Since 1980, the Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), the beloved bike-a-thon and the nation’s most successful athletic fundraiser, has seen plenty of both.

img.alt_text: Pan-Mass Challenge riders along the route

title.rendered: Teen Cancer America Partnership anniversary honored by rock legend Sir Roger Daltrey

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah
Photography by Sam Ogden

Legendary rock icon Sir Roger Daltrey, lead singer of The Who and co-founder of Teen Cancer America (TCA), visited Dana-Farber Cancer Institute on Aug. 26 to mark the 10th anniversary of Dana-Farber’s partnership with TCA. Daltrey spent time with teen and young adult patients as well as Dana-Farber staff, celebrating a decade of collaboration to improve care for adolescent and young adult cancer patients. Through the HomeGoods Young Adult Lounge, Dana-Farber’s Center for Young Adults provides vital support, connection, and creative programs. Later that evening, Daltrey performed in front of patients, faculty, and staff with his legendary bandmates at Fenway Park as part of The Who’s Farewell Tour.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Swim Across America
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Swim Across America’s Boston Open Water Swim raised $335,000 in 2025 to benefit patients who receive care at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and their families. Raising over $3.8 million since 1996, the organization continues to “Make Waves to Fight Cancer” and fuel critical survivorship research at Dana-Farber. This year's event will…

jetpack-related-posts.title: Dana-Farber researchers awarded American Society of Hematology funding
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The American Society of Hematology (ASH) funds groundbreaking research on blood and bone marrow disorders. Over the past year, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers have earned a total of $845,000 in competitive ASH grants.

jetpack-related-posts.title: OOFOS steps up for breast cancer research
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: In fiscal year 2023, active recovery footwear brand OOFOS donated $626,000 to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute through their Project Pink initiative, a special program that supports breast cancer research by donating a percentage of online sales to the Institute.

jetpack-related-posts.title: PopStroke
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: PopStroke completed its second annual October Breast Cancer Awareness Initiative, last year, in partnership with Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund. Throughout October, PopStroke locations nationally ran a number of initiatives to support breast cancer research and patient care at Dana-Farber, raising close to $145,000.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Dana-Farber team defies cancer in ASICS Falmouth Road Race
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On Aug. 21, more than 330 members of Dana-Farber’s team ran seven miles along the scenic Cape Cod coastline for the 50th running of the ASICS Falmouth Road Race.

img.alt_text: Falmouth Road Race Team Power runners

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

The Dana-Farber Society (DFS) is a group of visionary donors who are changing lives and creating a legacy through a planned gift such as a bequest, life income gift, or beneficiary designation to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, the Jimmy Fund, the Friends of Dana-Farber, or the Pan-Mass Challenge. DFS members provide a dependable future source of funding to fuel Dana-Farber’s pursuit of innovative treatments and bring hope to patients and their families. Planned gifts support the revolutionary research, extraordinary care, and groundbreaking physician-scientists transforming the way the world thinks about cancer.

Priorities fueled by members’ gifts: 

  • cancer prevention and early detection 
  • next-generation cancer drugs 
  • signature total patient care 
  • cancer care equity 
  • pediatric and young adult treatment 

Visit Dana-Farber.org/DFS or contact Planned_Giving@dfci.harvard.edu to learn more.

jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Dana-Farber Campaign has inspired pivotal planned gifts that will make a true difference for children and adults with cancer.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Trustees’ CGA helps fund the future
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Like many other financially savvy donors who want to make a difference far into the future, several Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Trustees are embracing the opportunity to establish charitable gift annuities (CGAs), including Jim and Barbara Sadowsky.

jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On May 24, more than 200 guests gathered at the Four Seasons Hotel Boston for the annual Dana-Farber Society Dinner.

img.alt_text: Attendees of the Dana-Farber Society Dinner pose for a photo

title.rendered: Expect Miracles Foundation honored with the Boston Red Sox Jimmy Fund Award

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Expect Miracles Foundation (EMF) received the 2025 Boston Red Sox Jimmy Fund Award—the Jimmy Fund’s highest honor—during a special on-field ceremony at Fenway Park. The presentation was a featured part of the annual WEEI/NESN Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon presented by Arbella Insurance. The award recognizes EMF’s extraordinary three-decade commitment to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s mission, with more than $1 million donated every year since 2018, and totaling over $15 million to support lifesaving cancer research. Through events like the East Coast Golf Classic, galas, and marathon teams, EMF rallies the financial services industry, and beyond, to fuel breakthroughs and provide hope for patients and families facing cancer.

Pictured (from L to R): Wally, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute President and CEO Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD, Jimmy Fund Co-Chairs Tom Caron & Brock Holt, Boston Red Sox President & CEO and Dana-Farber Trustee Sam Kennedy, Expect Miracles Foundation Founder & Chairman Frank Strauss (Cohasset), EMF Executive Director Frank Heavey (Chatham), and EMF Director of Development Maggie Dombroski (Manasquan, NJ) – photo courtesy Boston Red Sox.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Larry Lucchino receives Jimmy Fund’s highest honor
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The 2023 Boston Red Sox Jimmy Fund Award was presented to Chairman of the Jimmy Fund Larry Lucchino at a special Fenway Park ceremony in August.

img.alt_text: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute trustee Larry Lucchino with Dana-Farber CEO Dr. Laurie Glimcher

jetpack-related-posts.title: Boston Red Sox Jimmy Fund Award
jetpack-related-posts.author: Dana-Farber Impact
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The 2022 Boston Red Sox Jimmy Fund Award—the Jimmy Fund’s highest honor—was presented to John Berardi (second from right), program director of Jimmy Fund Little League presented by Franklin Sports, which rallies thousands of youth baseball and softball players each summer to fundraise for the Jimmy Fund in their communities…

img.alt_text: People on the field at Fenway Park

jetpack-related-posts.title: Two longstanding supporters receive the Jimmy Fund’s highest honor
jetpack-related-posts.author: Lori Dougherty
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The 2024 Boston Red Sox Jimmy Fund Award was presented to The Herb Chambers Companies and Team Beans at a special Fenway Park ceremony.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Rally Against CancerTM
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: On Opening Day at Fenway Park, Red Sox and Jimmy Fund fans celebrated by forming Rally Against CancerTM teams in their workplaces, schools, and communities, and raised $270,000 to defy cancer. Fisher Elementary of Walpole, Mass., and Northwestern Mutual Boston were the top fundraisers in a field of 52 Rally…

jetpack-related-posts.title: Red Sox name 2023 Jimmy Fund Captain
jetpack-related-posts.author: Colleen Sullivan
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Boston Red Sox pitcher, Garrett Whitlock, has been named Jimmy Fund Captain for the 2023 baseball season.

img.alt_text: Jimmy Fund Captain Garrett Whitlock in the Fenway dugout with pediatric patient Lily

jetpack-related-posts.title: Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon breaks records with $5.7 million raised for Dana-Farber
jetpack-related-posts.author: Hannah White
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The WEEI/NESN Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon presented by Arbella Insurance continued to be a beacon of support for Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund in August with a record-breaking fundraising year.

title.rendered: Lubin Family Foundation Scholar Award Annual Symposium

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah
Photography by Bryce Vickmark

Dana-Farber Cancer Institute celebrated its commitment to nurturing future leaders in academic medicine at the Lubin Family Foundation Scholar Award Annual Symposium, held on May 15, 2025. The event featured presentations from the 2023 and 2024 Lubin Scholar cohorts, showcasing their groundbreaking research. Nobel Laureate William G. Kaelin Jr., MD, Lubin Family Foundation Scholar Award Scientific Director, emphasized the importance of mentorship and financial support in launching successful research careers. The 2025 Lubin Scholar and Mentor cohort was announced at the symposium, highlighting the Richard K. Lubin Family Foundation and Dana-Farber’s dedication to retaining top physician-scientists. Keynote speaker Charles L. Sawyers, MD, an HHMI Investigator and leader in oncology and pathogenesis at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, inspired attendees with insights into advancing cancer research.

title.rendered: The Heather McMahon Glioblastoma Research Fund

content.rendered:
Winter 2025
By Casey Repasy

On June 30th, the family of the late Heather McMahon, including her parents, nieces, and nephews, attended a ribbon-cutting ceremony outside the laboratory of Jean Zhao, PhD, which revealed a plaque honoring Heather’s memory. The plaque honors the collaboration between Zhao and Patrick Wen, MD, Heather’s doctor, on glioblastoma research. Each year, the family hosts the “Storming the Greens for Heather McMahon” golf tournament, with proceeds supporting the Heather McMahon Glioblastoma Research Fund. The family also received a research update at the event. Since their last visit, the McMahon family has grown significantly, and Heather’s nieces and nephews appreciate opportunities like this to hear stories about their aunt.
